raw_findings.message: The flush token is a fixed source-code secret, so anyone able to reach the endpoint and learn the token can clear all stored values and counters.
Keys are truncated by byte count and lossily decoded, so distinct keys sharing the first 32 bytes can map to the same stored key.
The counter is read under one lock and written under a later lock, so concurrent increments can read the same value and overwrite each other's updates.
Adding an attacker-controlled delta to an i32 can overflow, wrapping the counter in release builds and panicking in debug builds.
Slicing a key at the prefix's byte length can split a UTF-8 character and panic while the map mutex is held, poisoning it and breaking later map operations.
The client-controlled destination is joined without restricting traversal or absolute paths, allowing snapshots to overwrite files outside the data directory.
Header bytes are appended to raw until a terminator arrives with no size limit, so a client can consume unbounded memory by sending an unterminated header.
A request line with fewer than two whitespace-separated fields makes these unchecked indexes panic the handler thread instead of returning a client error.
An attacker-controlled Content-Length is used to allocate the entire body without a limit, so a large value can exhaust memory or abort the server.
The percent-decoding slice can start or end inside a multibyte UTF-8 character, so a request target containing malformed percent encoding alongside non-ASCII text can panic its handler thread.
Snapshot failures are returned with the full filesystem path and underlying OS error, exposing server filesystem details to callers.
The query-controlled key is inserted into an HTML response without escaping, allowing a crafted URL to execute script in a visitor's browser.
Each connection gets a thread that can block indefinitely reading headers or a body, so clients that stall can exhaust the server's threads.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The counter key is attacker-controlled and written to stderr without escaping, so a key containing an encoded newline can forge additional log entries.
`fs::write` follows an existing symlink in the data directory, so a user able to create a symlink there can make a snapshot overwrite a file outside that directory.

A target containing a percent sign followed by an ASCII byte and a multibyte character (for example `%Aé`) makes this slice split a UTF-8 character and panic, terminating a worker; repeated requests can exhaust the worker pool.
Invalid UTF-8 percent-encoded bytes are replaced with U+FFFD, so distinct keys such as `%FF` and `%FE` decode to the same key and can overwrite each other.
The read timeout applies separately to each read, so a client that sends data more frequently than once every five seconds can hold a worker indefinitely and exhaust all workers.

raw_findings.message: The flush authorization token is embedded in the source, so anyone who knows the code can use it to clear the store.
Keys longer than 32 bytes are truncated, and truncating inside a multibyte UTF-8 character can also replace the suffix, causing distinct keys to alias.
An increment key containing decoded newlines is written directly to stderr, allowing a client to forge or inject log entries.
Adding an attacker-controlled delta to an i32 can panic in overflow-checked builds or wrap to an incorrect negative value in release builds.
The counter is read and later written under separate lock acquisitions, so concurrent increments can overwrite one another and lose updates.
The prefix length may fall inside a multibyte character in a stored key, making this string slice panic while the map lock is held and poison it.
The user-supplied snapshot path is joined without constraining it to the data directory, allowing requests to create or overwrite files outside that directory.
The server keeps extending `raw` until it sees the header terminator without a size limit, so a client can consume unbounded memory by sending an indefinitely long header.
A request line with no method or target makes these unchecked indexes panic the handler thread, so a client can trigger a crash with a malformed request.
The client-controlled Content-Length is used to allocate the entire request body without a limit, so an oversized value can exhaust server memory.
A percent escape followed by bytes that split a UTF-8 character can make this string slice panic, so a crafted URL can terminate its handler thread.
Snapshot failures return the filesystem error and full destination path to the requester, exposing internal path and OS details.
The unescaped query value is inserted into an HTML response, allowing an attacker to execute injected markup or script in a visitor's browser.
Each connection gets a thread that can block indefinitely reading a partial request, so enough stalled clients can exhaust server threads and resources.

The read timeout resets whenever a client sends more data, so a client that sends bytes just under every five seconds can hold a worker indefinitely and exhaust the fixed pool.

raw_findings.message: The admin flush token is embedded in the source, so anyone who knows the implementation can submit it to clear both in-memory maps.
Truncating keys to 32 bytes and converting an incomplete UTF-8 sequence lossily causes distinct keys with the same truncated prefix to map to the same stored key.
`incr` releases the counter lock between reading and writing, so concurrent increments can read the same value and overwrite one another.
Adding an untrusted delta to an `i32` can overflow, wrapping counters negative in release builds or panicking in debug builds.
Byte-length prefix slicing can land inside a stored key's UTF-8 character, panicking while the map lock is held and poisoning it for later requests.
Joining the untrusted snapshot destination without constraining it to the data directory lets `../` or an absolute path write snapshots outside that directory.
A client can leave a request incomplete indefinitely because reads have no timeout, occupying a handler thread per stalled connection until the server runs out of resources.
The server keeps appending input to `raw` until it sees the header terminator, so a client can send an arbitrarily large unterminated header and exhaust memory.
A request line with no method or target makes the input-derived `parts` vector too short, so indexing it panics and drops the connection without a response.
The client-controlled `Content-Length` is allocated before the body is read and has no limit, so a request declaring a huge body can exhaust server memory.
A percent sign followed by non-ASCII UTF-8 can make these byte-offset string indices fall inside a character, panicking the handler on a crafted request target.
Snapshot failures are returned verbatim to the client with the joined filesystem path and OS error details, exposing server filesystem information.
The decoded `key` query parameter is inserted into an HTML response without escaping, allowing a browser to execute attacker-supplied markup or script.

fixed_raw_findings.message: This timeout limits each blocking read rather than the total request duration, so clients that periodically send a byte can occupy all worker threads indefinitely and prevent the server from processing new requests.
Each distinct `/incr/{key}` request permanently adds a counter entry, and the maps have no capacity limit or eviction, so repeated unique requests can exhaust server memory.

A percent sign followed by an ASCII byte and a multibyte character (for example `%Aé`) can make this byte-indexed string slice end inside a UTF-8 character, panicking the worker and allowing repeated requests to deplete the worker pool.
